  not parse it and waits the configured time.
- Pi 0.87.0 and Antigravity: no usage-limit record was found, so their
  adapters report nothing new.

title: The Change page starts the planner on the server, and shows that it is working
goal:
On the phone today, planning a change means copying the hand-off block and
pasting it into a Claude Code Remote Control session on the server. With this
change, the hand-off block on the Change page gets a `Start planning` button
for an unplanned change, for Plan again before approval, and for Plan it on a
halted change. A tap starts the planner on the machine that serves the page,
in that machine's own tree, with its own harness login. The human never leaves
the osq page.

The tap runs `osq plan <id> --run`, the same command a shell can run. It starts
a detached osq process and returns at once. That process runs the planner the
way change 189's steering planner runs: the agent role's environment, osq
checks what it wrote, lints the plan, and records the outcome. A change that
needs steering is planned in place in its own osq worktree, exactly as 189
does. A change folder in the checkout is planned in a scratch worktree, and osq
copies back only the plan files, so nothing else in the checkout is touched.
This works the same in local `osq serve` and on the server.

While it runs, the change's next step reads
`planning (since <time>) — osq show <id>`, `osq approve` waits, and the Change
page shows `Planning on server · <n> min` instead of the hand-off block. When
the plan lints clean, the page moves to Approve. Any other outcome shows one
line saying what happened, above the hand-off block, which stays the fallback.

ADR 019 records the decision first. ADR 006 rejected headless planning, ADR
018 allowed it only for run triggers, and ADR 014 said no planner runs on the
server yet.

title: One ADR says how the dashboard is written, so executors stop learning its rules by failing
goal:
The dashboard in `packages/ui` has rules that are spread over one spec
requirement and two test files, and habits that are written nowhere. Change
192 task 4 died once on `scope_violation` because nothing told it how state
should cross a component it did not own; 194 task 7 dodged a timer ban with
`AbortSignal.timeout` because the ban was only a token list in a test.

This change adds ADR 020, which applies to web-inspection, so every planner
that writes web-inspection names it under `## Decisions` and every executor
reads it. Its rule: the dashboard renders server documents, logic sits in pure
model files, components only render, shared state uses React context, and no
state library is added. Its decisions cover data, files, state and tests, and
say when to revisit the state decision. It denies the common state,
data-fetching and router packages, so the watcher kills a task that adds one.

Its checks test, `tests/dashboard-writing-adr.test.ts`, enforces what can be
tested: the ADR record, the denied packages against the UI manifest, and the
view-file bans `tests/ui-change.test.tsx` holds today for
`packages/ui/src/change/`, widened to every screen folder and joined by
`AbortSignal.timeout`. The old scan moves into the new test and leaves
`tests/ui-change.test.tsx`. The one file that breaks the widened bans today,
`change/ChangeView.tsx`, sits on an explicit exception list that only shrinks.

title: A planned shared file recertifies its owner on every harness, and a passing scope regression offers retry
goal:
PLANNER.md promises that when a later task extends a file an earlier done task
owns, and has that file in its scope, the watcher recertifies the earlier task
by itself when its verify still passes. In 192 that did not happen: task 4
shared `ChangeView.tsx` with task 3, task 3's verify passed, and the change
halted with `scope_regression`.

The brief traced this to opencode's missing `file_changed` events. Planning
found a different cause. Automatic recertification does not read
`file_changed` at all. It follows the file through the later task's `measures`
end events. Task 4's first attempt died with `scope_violation`, and the worktree
discarded its edits, but its end event (`be20…` to `2f06…`) stayed in the
stream. The retry's end event starts again from `be20…`, so the chain had a gap
and the audit refused. A test that replays 192 under the current code fails
the same way, and passes once the discarded attempt's segment is dropped.

So this change:

- drops a discarded attempt's `measures` segment before the chain check, so
  a retried later task no longer breaks the owner's automatic recertification;
- credits a differing path from those same measured hashes when no
  `file_changed` event names it, records `source: "measures"` on that
  attribution entry, and keeps a typed event first;
- stops treating a `scope_regression` whose recorded verify passed as a
  steering trigger, so its next step, the inbox and dispatch offer
  `osq retry <id> <n>` (which recertifies in place) instead of `osq plan <id>`;
- adds a `recertifications` table to `osq query` to count credit sources.

title: osq lint refuses a delta that gives a capability a second scenario with the same name
goal:
`osq lint` reports an error when a change's delta would leave a capability with
a scenario name it holds twice, where the living spec held it at most once.
Today the planner finds out only when the first task's baseline goes red,
because `scenario()` lookups throw on duplicate names: 191 passed lint, then
every `scenario('web-inspection', …)` test threw on a second "Phone width", and
191 was rejected and replanned as 192.

title: A human keeps uncommitted edits as a manual change with one comment, and osq records them for the next planner
goal:
When `osq approve` or `osq land` stops on uncommitted edits in the human's
checkout, the human keeps them with one command and a comment:
`osq manual "<why>"`. osq commits them as a manual change, writes a record of
what they touched, and the stopped command can run again. `osq query` lists
the records, and the next plan prompt names the ones whose capabilities no
change has written since, so the planner can bring the specs in line. A
project that wants the old strictness sets `vcs.manualEdits: 'block'`.

title: One ADR says when osq may run an approved queue without a human
goal:
Today a human taps approve and land for every queue item, even when the whole
queue was shaped in one planner session. The next target, a fresh repository
rebuilt from an exported queue, should build from the first item to the last
with nobody watching. ADR 006, ADR 018 and ADR 003 stand in the way: they
reject headless planning for new changes, have a human approve every steering
revision, and write the default branch only through a command the human runs.

This change adds ADR 021, Autopilot, and nothing else. Its rule: with
autopilot on, a human approves the queue once; osq plans, approves, runs and
lands each approved item in order, and stops when recovery runs out. It
decides that autopilot is off by default and set per project; that
`osq queue approve` is the human gate, sealed by a hash of every item so an
edited item does not run; that autopilot plans with ADR 019's planner,
approves through `osq approve` and lands through `osq land`, and never skips
or overrides a gate; and the recovery ladder of automatic retries, then up to
`autopilot.maxSteers` steering rounds with ADR 018's planner, then a full
stop. It records how it amends ADR 003, ADR 006 and ADR 018.

`autopilot-queue-run` and `autopilot-recovery` build what it decides.

title: With autopilot on, the watcher plans, approves, runs and lands every approved queue item in order
goal:
ADR 021 decided an opt-in autopilot: a human approves the queue once, and osq
plans, approves, runs and lands each approved item in order. This change
builds it, without recovery, which is `autopilot-recovery`.

`osq queue approve` records the hash of every queue item in
`openspec/.run/queue-approval.md`, and `osq queue` shows which items it
covers. With `autopilot.enabled` in `osq.config.ts`, the watcher works the
first queue item that has not landed after each cycle, one step a pass:
`osq plan --next` creates its change, `osq plan <id> --run` starts the planner
of ADR 019, `osq approve <id>` approves a `ready` plan, the watcher runs the
tasks as always, and `osq land <id>` lands the archive. Each step calls the
command function itself, which the CLI hands to the watcher. A change
autopilot creates holds `.run/autopilot.md`, which names the item and the
queue approval it ran under and travels into the archive.

When a step needs a human, such as an unapproved or edited item, a planner
outcome other than `ready`, a refused approve, a halted change or a land that
stops, the watcher writes one stop record, `openspec/.run/autopilot-stop.md`,
with the reason and the one command that resumes the queue. `osq inbox`,
`osq status` and the dashboard show it. The queue stays stopped until a human
changes the state it stopped on or runs `osq queue approve`. All state is in
files, so turning autopilot off or restarting the watcher loses nothing.

title: The frozen-test gate protects a Rust project's tests, in each crate's tests folder and in test modules
goal:
An executor on a Rust project cannot weaken a preexisting test without
`tests.modify: true`, the same as on TypeScript. Today the frozen-test gate
protects only the root `tests/` folder, so a workspace crate's
`crates/<name>/tests/` and every `#[cfg(test)] mod tests { … }` inside a source
file go unguarded. After this change the Rust preset names its test folders as
data, the runner snapshots them through each path's nearest manifest, a new
languages adapter finds inline test modules with osq's own reader, lint flags a
crate test scoped without `tests.modify`, and the coverage list says the gate
covers Rust.

title: Verify lint accepts cargo commands and gives chain advice that fits a Rust project
goal:
A Rust project's task verify, such as `cargo test -p core --test parse`, lints
clean, and the chained-verify error tells a Rust project what to do instead of
naming package scripts it doesn't have. Today every `cargo` command draws the
"names neither an existing repository path nor a package script" warning, and
a chained verify is told to move into a package script even where there is no
`package.json`. After this change the Rust preset names `cargo` and its
subcommands as data, lint recognizes them in a project whose language map
holds Rust, the chain refusal suggests a script file when the root has no
`package.json`, and the coverage list says verify-command lint covers Rust.

title: The denied-dependency gate reads Cargo.toml
goal:
A task that adds a crate to a Rust project is checked against the
denied-dependency rules, as a package added to `package.json` is today. Today
the gate reads only `package.json`, so a crate added to any `Cargo.toml` goes
unchecked. After this change the Rust language adapter gains osq's own
`Cargo.toml` reader. It finds crates in every dependency table, follows
`package = "..."` renames, and refuses to guess on TOML it cannot read. The
watcher's baseline and comparison read scoped `Cargo.toml` files through it,
an unreadable manifest fails the gate with a message naming the file, and the
coverage list says the gate covers Rust.

title: The Rust core reads today's event logs into typed events, folds them into change state, and gates approve and archive by type
goal:
The Rust rewrite of osq starts with its core crate, `crates/core`, which is
empty today. Everything later reads change state through it: storage, the
loop, run, approve, archive and report. So the core types come first, with no
IO, and they must read the 79,000 event lines osq has already written exactly
as they are, because the rewrite keeps the archive instead of importing it.

After this change `osq-core` holds:

- the `Event` enum, one typed variant for each of the 35 event types today's
  TypeScript osq writes, with an envelope that reads and writes a JSONL line
  so that the JSON value of every archived line comes back unchanged, and read
  errors that never skip a line;
- `apply_task`, `apply_change` and `apply`, pure folds from a change's event
  streams to task and change state, and `change_status`, the status order
  TypeScript's `deriveSpecState` uses;
- `Seal` and `Change<Draft>`, `Change<Approved>`, `Change<Archived>`, so a
  change is approved only by a seal check and archived only when done, and
  the compiler refuses anything else.

title: The five Rust rebuild ADRs join decisions/, scoped to rust-core, with their checks
goal:
The Rust rewrite was designed in five ADRs on the Notion Rust Rebuild page:
feature crates and events, code style, link enforcement, the on-disk format,
and OpenSpec in Rust. Change 204 built the core crate under them, but they
are not in `decisions/`, so nothing in osq knows they exist. They could not
land earlier: scoped to `rust-core`, an ADR warns while that capability has
no living spec, and 13 ADR tests require osq's decisions to have no warning.
Since 204 archived, rust-core is living.

This change adds them as ADRs 022 to 026, numbered after TypeScript's 001 to
021, each `applies_to: [rust-core]` so they govern the Rust crates and not
`src/`. Each names a new `tests/rust-adrs.test.ts` in its `checks`, and ADR
022 and ADR 025 also name the 204 tests that enforce them: core does no IO,
and every archived event line round-trips. The ADR files are ready in this
change folder under `adrs/`.

title: AGENTS.md tells an executor how to work in the Rust crates
goal:
ADRs 022 to 026 govern the Rust crates, but they are scoped to rust-core,
and osq puts only ADRs that apply to all into AGENTS.md's project rules
block. A scoped ADR's rule reaches an executor only through the `## Decisions`
lines of the proposal it runs under. AGENTS.md's Layout does not list
`crates/`, and its Verify section names only `pnpm verify`. An executor
working in a crate learns the layer order, the doc and tag rules and the
verify script only from what each planner repeats, and change 204's task 1
spent three attempts on a cargo it could not find.

After this change AGENTS.md lists `crates/` in its Layout and gains a short
hand-written `## Rust crates` section after Verify. The section points at
the governing ADRs and states the working rules: Rust never touches `src/`,
layers go apps, then features, then kernel, then core, one crate is one
capability, every item has docs, functions and tests carry `Implements:` and
`Covers:` doc tags, tests live in the crate's `tests/` folder, workspace
lints are never loosened, and `sh scripts/verify-rust.sh` runs before exit.
`CLAUDE.md` is a symlink to AGENTS.md and follows it.

title: An ADR can apply to a capability group with applies_to group:<name>
goal:
An ADR's `applies_to` is `all` or a list of capability names. The Rust
rebuild ADRs 022 to 026 govern every Rust crate, about seventeen
capabilities by ADR 022's plan, but they can name only `rust-core` today. Each
new crate would have to be added to all five ADRs, and it cannot be added
before its change archives: an ADR naming a capability with no living spec
warns, and 13 ADR tests require osq's decisions to have no warning. So a
change that creates a Rust crate is not governed by the ADRs it must follow,
and lint does not ask its proposal to name them.

After this change an `applies_to` entry may be `group:<name>`, which names
every capability whose `osq.yml` sidecar has that group. That is the group
`capabilities.requireGroups` already makes every capability declare. A
capability that an active change creates counts through its sidecar in the
change folder, so the creating change is governed from the start. ADRs 022
to 026 move to `applies_to: [group:rust]`.

`Adr.appliesTo` keeps the entries as written, for display. A new
`Adr.governs` holds the resolved capabilities, and every reader that decides
governance reads it: `governingAdrs`, `systemWideAdrs`, decisions lint,
traceability `@adr` links, the system graph's `applies_to` edges and the ADR
docs page.

title: rust-core has no missed mutants, and a script and Rust CI check every crate with cargo-mutants
goal:
ADR 024 says `cargo llvm-cov` proves a test runs the code and `cargo mutants`
proves the test checks it. Neither runs anywhere today. A cargo-mutants 27.1.0
run over rust-core on 2026-10-18 made 117 mutants: 79 caught, 27 unviable and
11 missed, every miss a test gap. No test checks the text of four `Display`
impls, `Change::id` or `Change::tasks`. Two match guards in `apply_change` and
the tie guard in `TaskId`'s ordering can become `true`, and the `Done` arm of
`apply_task` can drop its `reason: None`, and no test fails.

After this change new tests in `crates/core/tests/` catch all 11, and one
script, `scripts/mutants-rust.sh`, runs cargo-mutants the same way by hand, in
Rust CI and in osq's check. It runs over the workspace, or over a diff's lines
when given a diff file, keeps its output out of the source tree, and fails on
a miss. Rust CI gains a blocking `mutants` job on each push's and pull
request's diff and a weekly full run, and ADR 024's Enforcement section says
so. rust-core owns the Rust tooling files, which nothing owns today.

title: A Rust change's verify fails on a missed mutant in the lines it changed
goal:
Since 208, Rust CI fails a push whose diff has a missed mutant. But osq lands
on main locally and pushes afterwards, so CI reports the miss only after the
change has landed, and nobody fixes it inside the task that wrote the code.

After this change, every verify osq runs for a change gets `OSQ_DIFF`, the
path of a temporary file holding the change's diff since `.run/base`,
untracked files included. osq writes it with the `vcs.patch` read it already
uses for dead tasks' patches, so the verify command never runs git: osq
alone touches git (ADR 003), and `OSQ_` variables already reach the verify
role (ADR 007). `scripts/verify-rust.sh`, the verify of every Rust change,
then runs `scripts/mutants-rust.sh` on that diff after the tests. A missed
mutant in the change's own lines fails the task's change-level verify, so
the executor adds the missing test inside its task. In CI and by hand, with
no `OSQ_DIFF`, the script says the mutation check did not run and passes, as
before; CI's own `mutants` job still checks each push.
